subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, March 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe for the second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Ross (Souris), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Wright.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext:
Last evening before the house adjourned I spoke for approximately fifteen minutes on this matter. I set forth, among other things, what I considered to be certain unavoidable conclusions that must be drawn from the discussions we have had on this topic. From those four conclusions, I would mention again three. First, the farmers raising wheat should have a twenty-five cents per bushel payment on the pool wheat from 1946 to 1950. Second, Britain is in no way obligated to pay any part of that twenty-five cents. Third, the Canadian government, therefore, should pay the twenty-five cents. I shall not review any of the things which I said concerning those matters

Canadian Wheat Board Act last night, but I wish to deal briefly with the first conclusion, that Canadian farmers should receive a final payment of twenty-five cents per bushel.
Some evidence on this question is to be gathered from a statement which is attributed to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). It is to be found in the Western Producer of November 13, 1950. The minister is alleged to have said that he did not believe the farmers in the west were being unreasonable. I do not believe the farmers of the west are being unreasonable, either. In the first place, the farmers went through a disastrous depression between 1929 and 1939. It is said that we all did, and that is quite true. For the farmers, however, the depression was more severe, I would imagine, than it was for most people. In a time of depression a farm tends to accumulate debt. If the farmer is going to recover, he must, in times of semi-prosperity, be free to gain sufficient to discharge that debt and rehabilitate himself.
All during the depression years the farmers were producing and selling wheat below the cost of production. They were looking naturally to the recovery of what might be called good times to re-establish themselves. Consequently, when the war came on and prices bid fair to rise, the farmers had1 a right to look to the improved prices as a means of. rehabilitating their farms. From the farmers' standpoint one of the main difficulties lies at this point. Just as soon as prices bid fair to rise above a certain level, the government intervened and prevented the farmers from profiting from the high prices.
The same thing was done in world war I. There was no disposition before world war II and during the depression for the government to intervene on behalf of the farmer to relieve the impact of those terrible depression years. The farmers were simply sold up. They were expelled from their land, those of them who were not able, somehow or other, to get by. As soon as it appeared that prosperity was about to return and that the farmer would be getting good prices, the government immediately intervened to prevent the farmer from doing so. Now, that is the first important consideration. When I say the farmers have gone through a disastrous depression, that is the general idea which I have in mind.
Last night the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) made a considerable point of the fact that prices were largely stabilized, and markets were stabilized, as a result of the United Kingdom-Canadian wheat agreement. That is true, and it redounds to the credit of the government. Apparently the government had in mindi stabilizing both 
prices and markets, and that is highly commendable. The difficulty which entered at this point was that whereas the farmers had good markets and reasonably good prices, the cost of production and the cost of living were permitted to rise, and that practically eliminated the advantage which the farmers had gained. In a general way the farmers feel that if the government has intervened to prevent them from profiting by the relatively high prices which might have prevailed during the war, and if at the same time the government has permitted freight rates to rise, the cost of machinery to rise and the cost of living to rise, and has seen fit to impose income taxes when the farmer does make a profit, then unquestionably the government has an inescapable responsibility to intervene to see that the farmers are not unduly penalized by the rising costs of production and living.
This principle was simply and clearly enunciated by me and agreed to by the member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) last night. If the munitions manufacturers were allowed1 during the war to have contracts under which they obtained the cost of production plus a just profit, then surely the farmers, who are producers of goods just as important as munitions, are not unreasonable when they also ask for a set-up which would give them the cost of production plus a fair profit.
There is a great deal of discussion throughout the country. We read bitter editorials here and there, and we hear radio commentators who, with respect to the problem, generate much more heat than light, confusing the issue and completely overlooking the fundamental basis of the whole contention of the western farmers.
I think it would be well to give just a sketchy indication of the increased costs under which the farmers are labouring and which they are unable to pass on. Before doing so may I point out that if a machine manufacturing company has its costs increased, it adds those costs into the ultimate cost of its product and makes the consumers pay. In the position in which the farmers find themselves, they are unable to do that; and this is an exceedingly important matter to keep in mind. Practically every other producer today in Canada, especially the manufacturer, is in a position to pass on his increased cost to the ultimate consumer. These producers are therefore in a better position than that occupied by the farmer.
Now I come to the farmers' cost: farm machinery, building materials, gasoline, oil and grease, feed, fertilizers, binder twine,

seed, hardware. These nine sets of commodities have increased in price between April, 1946 and August 1, 1950, as follows: In April, 1946, the index stood at 127-9; on August 1, 1950, the index stood at 194-3, an increase of 51-9 per cent. These figures I have taken from Labour Research of December,
1950,	to January, 1951, page 4, a document which I believe is unchallengeable as to accuracy.
As to farm living -costs, the farm living cost index stood at 126-1 in April, 1946. In August, 1950, it stood at 180-7, registering an increase of 54-6 in the index. This increase amounts to 43-3 per cent. These figures again are taken from the Labour Research bulletin or document, December, 1950, to January,
1951.
I now come to freight increases. One could deliver hours of discourse on the increases which have been permitted by this government to be brought into being by the railroads, all militating against the welfare of the western farmer particularly. I shall give only one item to show how seriously these freight rate increases have affected the farmers. During the past two and a half years livestock have had freight rate increases amounting to sixty-four per -cent. Thisl figure I draw from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture's submission of February 15, 1951, to the cabinet of Canada.
How do the farmers compare with the rest of the country with respect to their total over-all income? Are the farmers receiving their fair share of the national income? The answer is to be found in these figures. Twenty-five per cent of Canadians are living on the farm, -but the income of those living on the farm amounts to only between twelve and fifteen per -cent of the income of Canada. These figures quite clearly indicate that farmers as a whole across Canada are receiving just about one-half of what they ought to receive, when they are compared with the rest of the people of Canada as a whole.
Hon. members may say: What has the government to do with that? I would reply: What did the government have to do with it during the war, when they held the prices the farmers could receive down to a certain figure while they allowed the cost of production and distribution to increase? What did the government do about that? Just about everything. What could the farmers do about it? Just about nothing. If the government of a country that means to be well governed does not take care of a group as important as the farmers are, then the country is obviously not going to be on the way to that measure of prosperity which the 80709-77
Canadian Wheat Board Act resources of the country would justify one in expecting the country to enjoy.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext:
The next question is this. In the increase of prices which we are now suffering from, obviously the costs of food enter as an important determining item. To what extent are increased prices obtained by farmers for such things as milk, butter, potatoes, apples, and the like, and to what extent are those increases they are receiving entering into the over-all increase of costs? The farmers are not getting a higher share in proportion to the increase in the price of such things as milk. In order to go into that question and establish that fact scientifically one would have to indulge in considerable discussion which I think probably it is better that we do not go into at the present time. I think my statement can be supported completely.
There is one other matter which I wish to mention for the benefit -of all hon. members who find themselves in the position of the hon. member for Simcoe North. They are saying to themselves, particularly the Ontario and Quebec people: Well, we are the ones who are paying the taxes. This $65 million or $100 million or $200 million, or whatever it

Canadian Wheat Board Act is, is all coming out of us, and we cannot see why we should be for ever penalized in order to help out these western farmers.
Let me draw this very important matter to their attention. The best market that Ontario and Quebec have is western Canada. When western Canada prospers, there is full employment in Ontario and Quebec, and good times in Ontario and Quebec. If Ontario and Quebec desire to have prosperity, then they must be in a position, or they must take a position, in which they can ensure prosperity to the farmers of the west. I do not think there is a responsible member from Ontario or Quebec who would not confess the truth of that general statement.
Ontario and Quebec rule Canada. Ontario and Quebec members can outvote the members from all the other eight provinces by a margin of fifty. The result is that if anything goes wrong in this country, the responsibility for that error lies squarely on the shoulders of Ontario and Quebec. All the rest of us put together are unable to influence materially the decisions of the members of those two provinces. Men may try to laugh that off, but the grim reality of the truthfulness of it stands out to everyone who has given any serious thought to the conditions obtaining in this nation.
Therefore, if you are finding that the western farmers are in difficulties because of freight rates, the Ontario and Quebec members are to blame; for they can change the matter. If the western farmers are suffering from inflation, Ontario and Quebec members are the people who are guiding the government whose policies determine whether or not there shall be anything done about inflation. And so on, all through the whole list of the factors which affect the prosperity of Canada.
I say to the Ontario and Quebec members: If you choose to put the western farmers in a position in which they are not prospering, or are in danger of failing, then you must be prepared to pay out of your pockets the money which will tend to keep them from going over the cliff. There is not very much of a successful answer to that that the hon. member for Simcoe North can see. And so I do not hesitate to suggest that the money which is necessary to put the western farmers in a condition in which they can be a good market for Ontario and Quebec should be drawn from the revenues of Canada as a whole.
Let Ontario and Quebec people not imagine for a minute that they are paying all the costs. Income taxes weigh quite as heavily on the other eight provinces as they do on the people of Ontario and Quebec, and perhaps more heavily. The incidence of the


tariff on these provinces is far more onerous than it is on the people of Ontario and Quebec, and the incidence of freight rates is far more onerous on the eight other provinces than it is on Ontario and Quebec; this has been brought out time and again. And all the profits which are m-ade by the largest companies, in the main, pour into Ontario and Quebec. Go round the streets of Toronto and look at the great buildings you find there. Go into Montreal and look at the great buildings you find there. You cannot find buildings like them, or comparable with them, anywhere in the other eight provinces. Who has built those great buildings? The farmers of the west and the farmers of the east, of the other eight provinces, have built them. There is just no way of answering that argument. So let the Ontario and Quebec members not suppose for a minute that we are not paying our full share.
In passing may I refer to the amount of wealth which has poured into the Dominion of Canada as a whole as a result of the activities of the western farmers during the past years through wheat alone. Just read the speeches of certain hon. members. Read the speech of the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) who has set forth the amount of wheat that in world war II has been sold, and the amount that was received for it. All that money came into Canada to help to increase the prosperity of Ontario and Quebec as well as the other eight provinces. There is much wealth to be obtained from the eight other provinces of Canada if Ontario and Quebec will so manage that they can produce to their optimum.
I think I will say no more at the present time, Mr. Speaker, in respect of the justification for the request of the western farmers that there should be money appropriated to make up to them for the money which was taken out of their pockets as a result of the price fixing which prevailed during the war.
Having discussed that matter, I desire to proceed to the important question of the responsibility, or the .possible responsibility, of Britain for any share of that 25 cents. I see that my time is exhausted. I shall go on with that subject at the next available opportunity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not speak on this very important question in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, because I felt at the time that since the question was under discussion between the two governments some of the things I might have said might have hindered in some way rather than helped the negotiations going on between the two governments. Therefore at that time, although I was very anxious to speak on the matter, I chose not to do so. I did, however, outside the house and in whatever way I knew, advocate in every possible way a final payment of twelve cents. Since that time the decision of the government has been announced, and the discussion has been going on for a few days in this house.
In view of the confusing criticisms that have come from the opposition benches since the debate has started, and particularly in view of the "I told you so" attitude of many hon. members of the opposition, I thought I owed it to my constituents, the people I represent in this house, to state my view and indirectly the majority of the views of the people in my constituency.
Before I go on I should like to first establish the position taken by the various parties in this house at the time this agreement was signed. I think it is important, particularly in view of. the argument that has been put forward since then,
Those who were here at the time the agreement was presented to the house will recall that members of all parties and from all provinces raised no objection to the agreement being signed by the Canadian government. I know that since then members of the official opposition have said that they did not support the agreement, and for that reason I should like to place on the record the exact words of the then leader of the opposition, Mr. John Bracken, when he spoke on that occasion.* I quote from page 4811 of Hansard of August 14, 1946, as follows:

The farmers appreciate very much what has been said. Now we come to the contract itself. I must admit that I could not agree with the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher), for instance, who contended that the "have regard to" clause was a mysterious clause. To me the contract appeared to be very simple, and I believe that is the general impression that existed among the great majority of the farmers of the west. To me it is merely an ordinary open contract. A great many people are scandalized at our having signed an open contract. Nowadays-and this applied particularly to the period right after the last war-who can get a closed contract for anything? Only on
Canadian Wheat Board Act a very few things would anybody offer a closed contract. I know from personal experience that when I built a house I could not get a closed contract. The contractor agreed to a set price to build the house, but there was a "have regard to" clause in the contract which said that if the price of lumber or other materials went up I would have to pay the difference. Naturally prices did go up and I had to pay the difference. That was just an ordinary "have regard to" clause.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the very same thing was done with respect to the wheat agreement, except for one important point, that we did not name what percentage of the increase we would absorb or what percentage of the increase we would require the United Kingdom government to pay. The determination of the amount was left to the good will of the two countries, and you know that is something which is very hard to enforce. We recognized that, and I -agree with the Minister of Trade and Commerce that, so far as the whole contract is concerned, legally the United Kingdom is quite right in trying to maintain the position that it has no further payment to make. I am not suggesting -at this time that they broke the contract or that they are legally at fault.
However, if hon. members review the five years of the agreement I think they will be impressed by the fact that the farmers of western Canada have a real contention. What happened? When the agreement was signed it was for a period of five years, -and the price in the first three years was $1.55. Then comes the "have regard to" clause, which said that if prices went up or down the price to be set in 1948 would be adjusted accordingly. They did not say the price would be $2. That is what a lot of people forget. If the agreement had said that for the first three years the price would be $1.55 and for the next two years $2, then there would not have been any discussion about it, and the farmers would not have asked for more money. It would have been a closed contract, and on that basis that would have been that; but there was the "have regard to" clause. So in 1948, when the price of wheat was to be arrived at, there was a discussion between the two governments. At that time, when they came to the decision that they would pay $2 for 1948, a statement was issued. That was not just by the Canadian government or the British government; it was a joint statement by the two governments which said they were paying $2, and that regard would be had in fixing later prices. That statement was quite clear; it has been put on the record two or three times.

When the next year rolled around there was another discussion between the two governments; again a joint statement was issued to the effect that the settlement would come in the middle of 1950, which would be at the end of the crop year. Those statements always referred to the fact that a settlement would be made at the end of the five year period. Consequently the farmers of western Canada, and all their organizations, were led to believe that a settlement would be made and something would be forthcoming.

Now I submit that if on technical or legal grounds, at the end of the five year period, after all the wheat had been disposed of, both governments had suddenly decided that while there might be something in our claim still they were not tied down legally, it would have been a most unfortunate thing for a responsible government to do. Certainly I think it would have been breaking faith with a large section of our people who rightly or wrongly believed that a settlement would be forthcoming. To my mind there is no legal indebtedness, but there is a very real obligation, call it a moral obligation if you will or a matter of keeping faith, because of the publicity and the whole process that took place during those five years.
I am proud indeed that in spite of what has transpired the Canadian government has seen fit to recognize that moral obligation to a very large section of western Canada. It would have been a sorry thing if the government had completely ignored their plight. Just on this point I should like to refer to a paragraph in the Ottawa Journal of Saturday, March 10, which disturbed me considerably. It refers to this contract and offers more or less the same arguments I have presented, though in a slightly different way. Then it comes to this conclusion:
Therefore, to sum up, it is an evil thing for the Canadian government to be taking $65 million out of the Canadian treasury-which in fact it is doing -to hand over to Canadian farmers-and especially


evil when, doing this, they compound the wrong by saying they are doing it because Britain will not honour an obligation.
After reviewing the events as they took place, after reviewing all the statements that were made, I think it would have been a very evil thing if a responsible government had completely ignored those statements or even stood on perfectly sound legal and technical grounds in order to break faith with the people. After all, certain things are written and certain things are not, but they are all equally binding. In my opinion it was a question of keeping faith, and I am proud indeed that even at the cost of $65 million to the taxpayers of the country, this government recognized that obligation. The farmers of Canada have always trusted a Liberal government, and that fact had a great deal to do with this agreement being signed. The farmers might not have supported such an agreement but for that trust. They knew this administration would never break faith with them. The proof of the pudding is in the eating, and they had that trust as a result of what has taken place over the last twenty years.
Well, now, what does it mean to the taxpayers? In spite of the fact that $65 million is to be taken out of the treasury I submit that this is still the best bargain the taxpayers have had in our whole history as a nation. I do not want to go into great detail, but let us look at the subsidy angle in the matter of wheat. It has been pointed out already, and we all know, that from March 1945 to February 1947, though we were selling wheat to Great Britain at the reduced price of $1.55 and selling it at much higher prices outside the agreement, we were still bound to sell our wheat for Canadian consumption at $1.25. WeU, simple arithmetic shows that this price meant a loss of 30 cents a bushel, and I believe some 160 million bushels of wheat were sold at that loss. If you take $48 million lost to the farmers at that time, the remainder amounts to only a cent or a cent and a quarter, which is all we have to pay in order to keep faith with our people. So this contribution does not mean such a loss to the taxpayer. It has been made up to him many times by the fact that he obtained wheat at this price.

The wheat board, with whatever faults it may have, as well as the Canada-U.K. agreement, and the international wheat agreement, with their so-called drawbacks, have at least provided the producer with a guaranteed price, with all receiving the maximum price under the wheat board pooling operation.
Farther down it reads:
Farmers should realize, particularly the younger men, that in thirty-two crop years, on the Winnipeg grain exchange, only on two occasions did the high price for the year exceed the $1.83 which is the final payment under the five-year pool. And only in four years did the average price exceed $1.50.
These statements appeared in the Manitoba Co-Operator, as I said, of March 8. I should like to stress that point, and put on the record the annual message of the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, Mr. Hannam, in January of this year. Looking over the trend, he had this to say: The general trend of our Canadian farm program has been to try to eliminate as much as possible of the risk and gamble with which agriculture has been plagued in the past, and replace them with some reasonable measure of stability and security on a long-term basis. Extraordinary progress has been made in moving towards this goal even though it is difficult for some to appraise the security achieved. They should compare it with the insecurity of former years, rather than with occasional temporary gains of some who are outside the program. Mr. Speaker, I have listened with considerable interest to the opinions expressed by the various members on this wheat question. Down through the years that I have been here I suppose more time has been spent discussing the marketing of wheat than any other subject which comes before the house. Before I discuss some of the phases of the problem that are uppermost in, the minds of the people I have the honour to represent,
I should like to mention to the house-I regret that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is not in his seat at the moment- that last Wednesday the Prime Minister visited London, Ontario. While there he was given an honorary degree by the university of Western Ontario, which is situated in my riding. He also took time to visit the seed fair which was in progress in that city, put on by the Middlesex crop and seed improvement association, and which is the outstanding seed fair in the Dominion of Canada.
I am sure that he enjoyed his visit both to the university and to the seed fair.
Down through the years we have more or less had it laid down that, for the sake of good government, it would be necessary to have cabinet solidarity. But now we find the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) replying to a question of the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth (Mr. Charlton) asking if the same treatment as is proposed for the western wheat grower was going to be extended to the eastern farmer; and the answer was no. Then yesterday we heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) saying that the wheat deal was a closed book, that both Britain and Canada have fulfilled their 

agreements under it and there was nothing more to it. Then we heard that this "have regard to" clause was not being honoured. So we find that the cabinet is more or less split over this question. What are the people back home going to believe? What do they think about it?
If the Minister of Trade and Commerce were in his seat I think he would recall that last fall, at the time of the harvesting of the winter wheat in Ontario, a meeting was held in the city of Chatham, and at that time the government refused to implement the Agricultural Prices Support Act and support the price of winter wheat at that time. I said then, and I will say it again, that so far as the Agricultural Prices Support Act has been operative in this country, it was put on the statute books for one purpose and for one purpose only, namely to win two elections. As far as we are concerned, to date it has not amounted to a hill of beans Personally I am interested in the production of honey. The attempt to support the price of honey was an ill-advised scheme and it has depressed the price of honey for the next two years instead of helping it. Whoever was the "brains" back of it should certainly revise his thinking a little bit, because it was the worst scheme I have ever seen in operation.
During this session the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and I entered into a little argument over a statement regarding the production of sugar. A statement was made in Chatham and then another statement was made in the house. It seems to me that they use one argument in the country, as it suits the country, and then come into the house and correct that. Those things have been, going on. The farmers have always wanted stability. Now that they have got stability it seems to me that they find it profitable to repudiate their negotiators. The farmers also forget that the taxpayers of Canada made a loan to Great Britain of $1,250 million which in effect was used to buy this wheat. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said last night that ECA funds are involved, and it is all mixed up but the fact remains that we lent them $1,250 million. More than that was spent on wheat, and the Canadian taxpayers were very glad to make the loan for that purpose.
There has been a lot of fuss about a subsidy to the Canadian domestic market during the war. Is it forgotten that during the .var every other primary producer in Canada also subsidized the Canadian consumer? Up until 1947 we never obtained for lumber or fish anything like the world price. I know of one member of the cabinet, for instance, who until 1947 was not able to obtain any more for his product than he. received in 1939. That is true of a great many manufacturers in Canada, and I think sometimes the wheat producers forget that fact.
As the Minister of Trade and Commerce said last night, the farmers elected to take out insurance. They wanted the government to put a floor price under their product. Now they are balking at paying the premium for it. Not only are they balking at paying the premium, but they want the Canadian taxpayers generally to pay the premium. Personally I do not go for that.
We hear so much about wheat in this house. There is talk about 40-cent wheat and 30cent wheat. The farmers sometimes forget that we had very low prices in British Columbia about the time when they were
Canadian Wheat Board Act getting 30 cents or 40 cents for their wheat. I can remember well fishing herring as a boy 'and delivering at the plant for one-ninth of a cent a pound. I fished salmon, and delivered it to the plant for one-third of a cent a pound. As a matter of fact wheat never got below half a cent a pound. If the farmers want to come and see how hard it is to wrestle a bushel of salmon or herring let them come out there and they will be able to judge the relative value. I tell you that your prices did not go as low as ours did at that time.
The lumbermen and fishermen elected to sell their own products. They did not want floor prices under them. Now they are asked to pay the premium for the farmers who wanted floor prices. I wonder "whether the farmers appreciate the value of holding on to a market? I wonder whether they realize that at the present time the pulp and paper companies of Canada are actually losing tens of millions of dollars every year in order to fulfil their contracts and obligations to their very good customers in the United States. If they wanted to enter the free market for pulp and paper at the present time I am sure they could sell a great deal of their product at probably $300 a ton. Of course that would net them a lot of money. But from the long-term point of view they probably feel it would not be to their advantage.

Mr. Speaker, Bill No. 117 is an act to incorporate Canadian-Montana Pipe Line Company under the general pipe line legislation passed by this parliament. The object of the company is the construction of a pipe line from the southeastern portion of the province of Alberta to the Montana border to meet an existing pipe line there. The pipe line will carry natural gas and will be approximately thirty-six miles in length. The incorporators named in the bill are the principal executive officers of the McColl-Frontenac Oil Company Limited and of the Montana Power Company of Butte, Montana. McColl-Frontenac Oil Company Limited of course is well known in Canada. The Montana Power Company is a public utility company which since 1931 has been distributing natural gas to domestic, commercial and industrial users in that state.
One of the chief, in fact the chief, industrial customer of this company is the Anaconda Copper Mining Company, which, as hon. members know, is a very important contributor of base metals so essential at this time.
From 1941 until last year approximately fifty wells were drilled in the area to which I have referred, and as a result four relatively small natural gas fields were proven in what is known as the Pakowki lake district. The most northerly, called the Manyberries field, lies within thirty miles of the United States-Canadian border, and the most southerly called Black Butte within a mile and a half of the Alberta-Montana border.
The opinion is held that the taking of gas from the Pakowki district will not particularly affect Alberta's supply inasmuch as these fields represent a small fraction indeed of the total Alberta reserves, and inasmuch also as they constitute a fixed limited quantity. We are not dealing here with a speculative venture. These fields are under the control of the incorporators. This application therefore will differ from those of other companies that hope to export to expanding markets, and therefore the quantities necessary for those companies will be much larger.
In any event the purpose of this bill is merely to incorporate a company. If the bill is passed and the company is incorporated it will be subject to the decisions of, and the usual safeguards provided by, the several regulatory bodies. Hon. members are familiar with these safeguards. I shall only enumerate them. First, under the general Pipe Lines Act the board of transport commissioners was authorized to regulate interprovincial or international pipe lines. Second, before gas


can be exported a permit must be obtained from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act. Third, before gas can be exported from Alberta a permit must be obtained from the Alberta petroleum and natural gas conservation board. Several applications have been made to that board and are still pending.
Therefore if this company is incorporated parliament will only be giving the company the same chance it has given other companies, -the chance to prove its case, to fight it out with these other companies and to show that the building of the proposed pipe line is for the benefit of Canada. I submit that only if there are a number of companies in competition presenting a variety of routes and schemes will Canadians be assured that what is finally decided upon will be in the best interests of our country.
The bill contains the same clauses and provisions, and is in the same form, as other pipe line bills which have been considered by this house from time to time. Detailed information and expert evidence will be available to the committee to which the bill is referred.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to delay the passage of the bill for very long, and I think I should say at the beginning that I do not intend to oppose passage of it at the second reading stage at any rate. Coming from southern Alberta, and having read the proceedings before the Alberta petroleum and natural gas conservation board involving this particular company, with deference I think I am probably as familiar with the project, what it is intended to do and the other factors involved, as anyone in the house.
There are a few facts which I think should be put before the house with respect to the company. The first is that the field from which it is intended to take the gas is in the very southern part of Alberta. It is a comparatively small field sometimes known as Pendant d'Oreille but more generally as Pakowki lake field. I believe the total amount of gas estimated to be there is in the neighbourhood of four hundred billion cubic feet.
Representations made before the Alberta petroleum and natural gas conservation board on behalf of this company were to the effect that probably the only place this gas could ever be marketed would be to this Montana Company which would like to pipe the gas a comparatively short distance to connect with the Montana grid system. There may be a considerable amount of truth in that argument.

There are, however, three other places where the gas may be used and may be required. The Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Company whose bill was before the house the other day, and who presented their case before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, gave a certain amount of evidence with respect to the use of this field. The effect of it was that they felt they needed this field if their project to build a pipe line from Alberta to Toronto and Montreal went through. I asked several questions in connection with the use of this field because I knew this bill was coming up, and the officials of the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Company gave evidence that they hoped and intended to take about forty million cubic feet a day out of this field if their project was approved and went through. They did say under questioning, also, that no field in Alberta was absolutely essential to their project with the exception of Pincher Creek field; but they felt they would probably need the gas in this field as a reserve, at least at present.
In addition another company which obtained a charter some time ago, the Western Pipe Lines Company, whose project is to pipe gas from Alberta to Winnipeg through Moose Jaw, Regina and the other cities along that route, look upon this field as more or less essential to that project. Whether or not it is essential I do not know, but at any rate they feel this field would be essential to their development which, of course, is primarily to serve western Canadian cities.
There is a third possibility for the use of this gas; that is, by the city of Calgary and the southern part of Alberta served by the Calgary Gas Company. My understanding is that the Calgary Gas Company does not require this gas at the present time, but unless other reserves are developed it may be that some time in the future it will require it.
I do not suggest that these people who have developed the Pakowki lake field, who have drilled wells and spent a considerable amount of money in developing these gas reserves, should be held up indefinitely because at some time in the future that gas may be required by someone else. However, when this bill is considered by the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, I do believe the factors I have mentioned very briefly this evening should be gone into carefully. They may have an extremely important bearing upon whether or not this charter should be granted. I have no doubt, of course, that these matters will be considered carefully if the charter is granted and the company makes application to the Alberta

Border Pipeline Corporation conservation board. My position last year was and still is that in considering these pipe line charters the members of this house have a duty and responsibility to the people of Canada as a whole to carefully look into the proposition put forward, to consider its feasibility and whether or not it is going to be in the best interests of the country as a whole. So I believe the three possible uses to which this gas might be put other than sending it across to Montana essentially, as I think the sponsor said, for the use of the Anaconda Copper Company, should be gone into by the committee and given a good deal of attention.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. A. Robinson (Simcoe East) moved
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 118, to incorporate Border Pipeline Corporation.
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, the continuing discoveries of oil in the province of Alberta have brought to the fore various proposals for the construction of an oil pipe line from the province of Alberta to the Pacific coast. The discussion of this project has been accelerated by certain considerations of national security in the United States and Canada. At the present time oil for Vancouver and the province of British Columbia, as well as that used in Portland, Seattle and the northwestern part of the United States, is furnished largely by tanker from the state of California. In the event of a war the supply of oil from California might not be sufficient to continue to service these markets, thus making it desirable to call upon the large resources of Alberta in this connection. Furthermore, the hazards of transportation of oil by tanker during a war also indicate the desirability of a pipe line as a means of providing oil to these markets.
In the light of these considerations this application is being made to parliament for the incorporation of a company under the provisions of the Pipe Lines Act with authority to construct and operate an oil pipe line. It is proposed that this line will commence in the vicinity of Edmonton in central Alberta and run south in that province, then parallel to the Canadian Pacific Railway through the Crowsnest pass to Cranbrook and Kingsgate
1210	HOUSE OF
Border Pipeline Corporation in British Columbia where it will cross the border and proceed southwest to Spokane along the route of the Spokane International Railway. The route of the pipe line then runs west across the flat plains of the state of Washington, through Steven's pass and the Cascade mountains to Monroe and Seattle, from which point the line divides in two directions. One section of the line runs north 115 miles to Vancouver, and another section 190 miles south to Portland.
The applicants have entered into negotiations with United States and Canadian oil companies which have interests in the province of Alberta to supply the necessary oil to maintain the pipe line. It is also expected that they will obtain commitments to build sufficient refining capacity in Vancouver and in Seattle and Portland to market the "throughput" of the pipe line. The pipe line will have an initial "throughput" of 100,000 barrels per day and would have a capacity in excess of 150,000 barrels per day. The line will be a common carrier available to any producer who wishes to transport oil.
The applicants have entered into arrangements with prominent Canadian and United States investment firms which have indicated their willingness to undertake the financing of the pipe line through the sale to the public of the securities involved, both in Canada and the United States.
It is believed that the proposed pipe line, because of the lower cost of construction on the route proposed as opposed to any other suggested route and because of the wider market afforded by the sale in United States cities along the suggested route, will provide oil in the cities of Vancouver and New Westminster at a lower price per barrel than could be provided under the terms of any *competing project. It is on this basis that the applicants seek the right to have their plan for the construction of the pipe line placed before the board of transport commissioners and as a first step to have the company incorporated under the provisions of the Pipe Lines Act.
May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that by reason of the Pipe Lines Act which was enacted in 1949 parliament has said to any person who wishes authority to construct or operate pipe lines that he must come to parliament and make application for a special act. I believe our function under the overall act is quite clear; it is to grant or refuse incorporation. Once incorporation has been granted, questions of route and other matters must be decided by the board of transport commissioners. The company cannot begin construction of the line until the board has granted leave. Similarly, no line can be


opened for the transportation of oil or gas until leave has been obtained from the board. Therefore these present applicants are only doing what parliament has indicated, they must do. They are coming to parliament to seek incorporation.
In 1949 five pipe line companies were incorporated, and in/the 1950 session there were	two others. At this session I
believe there are seven applications under	the Pipe Lines Act. At the
present time companies to which this parliament has already granted incorporation have two applications for the construction of oil lines and four applications for the construction of .gas lines pending before the board of transport commissioners. If incorporation is granted in this case, and I hope it will be granted if we .are to avoid, discrimination, this company will then proceed to make its application to the board of transport commissioners. It will then be in a position to compete with other companies already incorporated or to be incorporated, for the right to construct and operate a pipe line. The applicants fully realize that they will only be successful in that competition if they are able to convince the board that their project is the most advantageous from a Canadian point of view.
Mr. Speaker, I have made my explanation as brief as possible. I would be very happy to answer any questions of a general nature when closing the debate. Expert witnesses will be available before the committee to answer questions of a technical nature.
May I ask the hon. member one question for the sake of clarification? Is it proposed that this pipe line will run through any part of the Fraser valley? If it does not, I think you are in trouble.

Mr. Speaker, this bill seeking incorporation of the Border Pipeline Corporation represents the second occasion on which there has been before the house a bill to incorporate a company which proposes to transport oil from the fields of Alberta to the Pacific coast. The first one came before us last week when a bill was introduced by the member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing). Last session, and the session before, we did have a number of bills from companies seeking incorporation who desired to build gas pipe lines from the prairies to the coast. This is the first session at which we have had 'bills to incorporate companies building oil pipe lines. But, Mr. Speaker, the principle which should be followed with regard to the use to be made of these Canadian resources, which is that, when works of major national importance are to be built to transport Canadian natural

resources to the market, they should be so constructed as to be of a maximum benefit to Canada, is I think the same in the case of both oil and gas pipe lines. The controversy which was before this house during the past two years in connection with gas pipe lines, therefore, is exactly the same as the controversy which will undoubtedly surround the application to incorporate this company.
The hon. member who introduced the bill said something to the effect that his company maintains that the route they have chosen to the Pacific coast via the United States will be the cheapest route to construct. I do not agree that we have had any figures which would warrant one in coming to that conclusion. Against the hon. member who introduced this bill I would set the member for Vancouver South and the great construction company-so he described it and I have no reason to doubt his description-which he states is to build the pipe line for his company. This company has had a great deal of engineering experience, not only in Canada and the United States but all over the world. It has investigated the routes from the prairies to the markets to be served on the Pacific, and has decided that the route through the Yellowhead pass, down through the centre of British Columbia to the Pacific coast, is a feasible and economic route for this pipe line to follow. Mr. Speaker, if one investigates the history of pipe line construction, and if one were to remember the things that were said in this house during the main session of 1950 concerning the impossibility of building a pipe line through the Yellowhead pass, through the centre of British Columbia to Vancouver and then into the United States, one could not help but be struck by the lack of information upon which those statements were based.
In his speech during the introduction of his bill the member for Vancouver South alluded to the history of the company which proposes to build that line, and its construction of pipe lines in Iran and the Middle East. If you look at those pipe lines and the altitudes that they reach during their course from the oil fields to the seaport, you will find that they go over mountain passes considerably higher than anything on the route of the Yellowhead pass and along the Hope-Princeton route to Vancouver. I understand that the pipe lines in the Middle East, in Iran particularly, reach altitudes of between
6,000	and 7,000 feet. There would be nothing like those altitudes on the route through the Yellowhead, so there is no reason, either because of the physical geography or economic conditions due to the difficulty of
Border Pipeline Corporation construction, which would mean that the pipe line seeking to bring Alberta oil to the Pacific coast need be built, or should be built, for the major part of its length through the United States.
We who took the position in the past, and who also take the position today, that in using these Canadian resources the maximum benefit must be preserved to Canada, were encouraged when the first pipe-line company to come before this house for incorporation this year adopted a Canadian route. We were also encouraged by the support which appears to be building up for the principle of Canada first, not only in this house but throughout the country. We recall of course that when we first asserted that principle-and I am looking of course at my good friend the member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) who took such a part in the fight for Canada first; the member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green); and the members for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and Yale (Mr. Jones)- the use of the term "filibuster" was applied to the efforts we made to impress upon this house and the country the importance of the principle which we were asserting. It is a fact which the reading of Hansard will verify that our efforts were greeted with-well, at first derision. I do not think that is too strong a word to use. Certainly every pressure was put upon us to end that filibuster. Every effort was made to have us withdraw our opposition to those companies seeking to export Canada's gas first to the United States and to build the route through the United States. We are therefore happy indeed, Mr. Speaker, that we have made such a large number of converts, if I may put it that way.
We recall that when the matter was held up last in the House of Commons and full discussion was insisted upon, as more and more members entered the controversy-not only members from British Columbia but members from other parts of Canada not immediately affected by the pipe line itself- it became apparent that a great national principle was at stake. That national principle had its recognition, I think, in the resolution that was moved the other day in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines and was adopted unanimously by that committee, to amend the provisions of a proposed bill to incorporate one of these pipe line companies to provide that "the main pipe line or lines either for the transmission or transportation of gas and oil shall be located entirely within Canada." That was an amendment moved on March 8 by my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and unanimously

Border Pipeline Corporation adopted in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. That, Mr. Speaker, represents almost a revolution in thought as compared with what we saw in this house and in that same committee just last year. I should like to take this opportunity of paying my tribute to those of my colleagues who took such a prominent part in carrying on that fight in the interests of the Canadian people.
I have dealt with that matter in these few sentences because I think it is important to remember that exactly the same issue is now before the house: that is, whether we shall grant our approval to bills which seek to incorporate companies which have as their avowed aim and object in the construction of a line to transport this resource to the market, that it shall go immediately and directly into the United States, and then through the United _ States for the greater portion of its length on its way to that market, with merely a branch or spur line back up to Canada to serve the market on the Canadian portion of the Pacific coast.
I will not say much at this stage in connection with the potential benefits which would flow to the cities in the interior of British Columbia, if the pipe line were built by a route through the central portion of the province, but which will be denied to us if it goes through the United States, because perhaps the situation with respect to oil is slightly different from the situation with respect to gas. No one can say definitely that it would be possible to tap the oil from the main pipe line and serve the communities through which that line passes. But neither can anyone say that it would be impossible. No one knows what the economic development of our province may be in the near future. No one knows the tremendous bounds forward which we may make. Those communities have been growing-many of them have doubled their population since just before the last war. They have been growing at an amazing rate. It may well be that before many more years go by there will be in the interior portion of our province a market sufficient to justify some plants, at any rate, to deal with this crude oil which will be flowing through the pipe lines. The importance of having that line through Canada becomes obvious, so that Canadian cities and communities will be in a position to derive the maximum benefit not only from the construction of the line but from the very presence of the line and the proximity of the resource which it carries.
I think we would be betraying our trust and be derelict in the duty that we owe to the Canadian people if we did not put forth every effort to make certain that these advantages are not forever lost to Canada and

forever secured to another country. On that basis I do not see that there is any course open to us-particularly to those who took the same stand in connection with the gas pipe lines-but to oppose the incorporation of a company such as this which proposes to follow the route which has just been set forth by the hon. member who introduced the bill in this house.
Not only does the fact that the line should be located within our country become a matter of great importance to the future development of that section of the country, but also the benefit which would follow from the construction of the line itself is a matter which this house should not allow itself to lose sight of. After all, it stands to reason that, if a company which is controlled by American capital obtains a-charter to build this line for the major portion of its length through the United States, it will employ Americans to build it, it will use American steel, and all the benefits of construction and maintenance, including roads which must be built in order for them to lay the line, will go to the United States; whereas if we have the foresight and the determination to insist that these benefits shall be preserved for Canada, then we would have those benefits to contribute to the economic development of this country.
There is at least a possibility if not a probability that, under the policy I am advocating, Canadian steel would be used in the construction of the line. Certainly it must be a fact that Canadian men would be employed in the construction of the line through Canada whereas Americans would be employed in the construction of the line through the United States. The same thing applies with respect to the pumping plants and the maintenance plant. These pipe lines require pumping stations at frequent points along their length. Each pumping station requires men to maintain it, to run it and to supervise it. Then there are the line men working on the maintenance and the regular inspection of the line itself. Are these men to be Americans or are they to be Canadians having the advantage of the employment which follows from the development of a Canadian resource? Surely hon. members of this Canadian House of Commons, this Canadian parliament, can come to no other conclusion than that these benefits and these advantages should flow to the country which they serve and whose people elected them as their representatives here to look after their interests. Hon. members can be quite certain that if they do not insist that this line and1 any other line be built through Canada first, so that the resource shall serve Canada first, then those benefits will flow to the United States and

will be forever denied to this country, with the consequent result of even further magnifying the disproportion which now exists between the economic development of the United States and that of Canada.
On that basis, Mr. Speaker, I am content to rest my case; and I appeal to this House of Commons, which showed that it is sensitive to public opinion and which, as a matter of fact, I think showed a good deal of patience when, last year, we were advocating principles to which at that time the majority of the members were not sympathetic. I do appeal now to hon. members of this house, since I am encouraged to believe they appreciate more fully the importance of the principle of the national interest to be served, to assert themselves on this occasion in the interests of Canada in connection with this line, and refuse to give their consent to the incorporation of any company which does not give its undertaking to build its line in such a way that it will serve Canada first.

Sheik of Araby collects $40,000 daily from oil-rich desert

Border Pipeline Corporation Saskatchewan, and even in Ontario. But I want to make clear what goes with an oil well. I quote:

I will admit that we westerners would be in a more fortunate position than some from the central provinces in caring for a harem in more ways than one.
Last year, Mr. Speaker, as the previous speaker said, we were accused of staging what they called a filibuster in connection with pipe lines. Those of us who took part in the debate felt that we were unfairly accused of carrying on a filibuster, but we are extremely proud of the fact that we took part in those debates, and I shall tell you why. We are proud of the fact, if for no other reason than that certain of my colleagues both from the glorious province . that I come from and even from the lesser provinces now realize the fact so eloquently portrayed by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) the other night when he introduced a bill, backed 1 presume by very responsible people, if I understood him correctly, and I think I did. I congratulated him when he introduced his bill the other night and I do so again tonight for the same reason, namely, that he implied, and I have every reason to believe he will back it up when it comes before the committee, that the amendment referred to by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) would be accepted. It is of such vital importance that I shall put it on the record again. This is the amendment moved last year by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green):
Provided that the main pipe line or lines, either for the transmission or transportation of oil or gas, shall be located entirely within Canada.
That, Mr. Speaker, is all that we are interested in. I had better take a moment
1214

Border Pipeline Corporation to congratulate the sponsor of the bill tonight on the excellent attempt he made in putting a very poor case before the members of this house. If he will say tonight that he will adopt the amendment, go further than that and have it inserted into his bill, as one company has done already owing to the magnificent effort of a few of us last year, providing for an all-Canadian route, there would be no difficulty about it.
Some of my colleagues may not as yet appreciate what Canada means nOw or what it could mean in the future. I am going to read all of this, Mr. Speaker, before I am through this session. I do not know of any better authority that I can quote when speaking, particularly in this house, but in so far as I am concerned, when speaking before the people anywhere in Canada, than our present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I will be glad to quote him in full but I do not want to take up too much time tonight, Mr. Speaker. I shall quote a part of his remarks as follows:	.
It is not only the people of Quebec and New Brunswick who have deplored the fact that the Canadian Pacific had to run through Maine to get to New Brunswick: that was something which concerned the people of the whole dominion. It was because of their feelings in that respect that the Canadian National took the long course through the valley of the Matapedia adding a great many miles to the distance. Nevertheless they provided an all-Canadian route. It was for that reason that the route traced for the transcontinental railway when it was built some forty years ago goes through the county of Temiscouata and into New Brunswick without departing at any time from Canadian soil. That is a thing which I think is of satisfaction to us all.
That is exactly what we endeavoured to do last year in connection with pipe lines, and . what a few of us at least intend to do this session. I might quote something about the sheik of Araby, but I do not think you. would want me to. Those who are fighting for an all-Canadian route are doing so to benefit their own province and Canada as a whole. No threats or inferences or anything else will deviate us one inch from the path we are following in an endeavour to build up our own province first, along with the entire economy of Canada.
We would like our friends, not only from our own province but from the other provinces, to support this amendment. I should like to hear any member of any party from any province get up on a platform in British Columbia and repudiate this amendment. From the political point of view there is no candidate representing any party who could appear in British Columbia and say that he opposed this amendment. We are not doing
[Mr. CruickshankJ

this for that reason; we are doing this because we know it is going to build up British Columbia.
Last year it was suggested by the president of a company which wanted to build a United States route-his name was either Nixon or Dickson, a promoter from the United States- that industry does not follow a pipe line. Yet ten days later the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) stated that the United States munitions board or those entrusted with trying to speed up the production of munitions in that great country had asked him to expedite the export of gas into Idaho and Washington. Does that not prove that industry does go with a pipe line? Does not that prove that we should use this gas to promote industry within our own country in these trying times, to build up stockpiles of munitions and other things needed for defence?
I do not think there should be a dissenting voice in this house, irrespective of where the member comes from, when this amendment is put before it. There is one thing to the credit of this company and that is that they have admitted openly that they are going through Kingsgate, down to Spokane, thence to Seattle and then to Vancouver. No doubt I shall have an opportunity to speak again on pipe lines before this session is over. I do not want to take one minute after nine o'clock to press this matter unduly.
I want to salute the premier of Alberta as a Canadian for having stated that no gas or oil will be permitted to be exported until the needs of Canada are met. He deserves every credit for making that statement. I would like to have some of the money coming from the oil wells. I do not understand the money they suggest in Alberta, but I certainly would like to know something about the money that comes from these oil wells.
There is not a solitary soul in British Columbia who wants this United States route. Everyone realizes that hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars are at stake. Every time four or five men can get $80 or $100 together to buy a few pieces of stationery they apply for a charter. The Rockefeller fortune was not made from oil that came from the ground; it was made from the transportation, distribution and sale of oil.
It is inconceivable to me that anyone would want to build up the great country to the south before our own needs are met. It was said last year that some of us do not want gas or oil exported to the United States. That is an argument you would expect to be advanced from the corner from which it was advanced. In a gathering of

262 there is bound to be at least one who cannot understand anything at all. We want to export our surplus to the great country to the south, but we do not want to send our gas to the United States and then back into the great port of Vancouver.
This matter could be easily solved by this company doing what the Trans-Canada company did. I do not see how they could do otherwise. I am sure that the hon. member for Vancduver South (Mr. Laing) will speak after me on this particular bill and with his usual eloquence. When he spoke so eloquently the other night in connection with another pipe line bill he said he was interested in the welfare of his own province. I am proud that he comes from the great city of Vancouver. He has told us that the company whose bill he is sponsoring is going to bring its gas and oil into that great city. This will be greatly appreciated at a time when it is needed for national defence purposes.
I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

Mr. Speaker, after the eloquent speech we have just listened to I am afraid that my dissertation on wheat will not be particularly interesting to this house. It was stated on a previous occasion, and I think it should be repeated, that of the 262 members there are only 42 who indicated themselves as farmers on their ballot papers. There are roughly only 52 members who are either wheat farmers or who represent wheat farmers. Despite that fact hon. members in every corner have been listening to what has been said on behalf of the western farmers and I trust they will forgive me for taking a little more time in this debate.
I happened to be on the train that came down to Ottawa in February of 1942. I think I was the only member of this house who was on that train which carried a delegation down here to ask the government under the late 80709-781
Canadian Wheat Board Act Right Hon. Mackenzie King to give us $1 per bushel for our wheat. In fact, there were two trainloads of delegates. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Whiteside) is now a sitting member but at that time there was no other member of any house, provincial or otherwise, who was on those trains. We received splendid treatment in Ottawa. We put forward a case at that time asking for one dollar wheat, and we finally got 90-cent wheat. I think it is just as well that we refresh our memories about what happened on that occasion. There was not a C.C.F. member of parliament on either of those trains, not one of them, and they had C.C.F. members of parliament at the time.
I want to say further, and I am going to bring you up to date now, that after listening to the different speakers in this debate I shall quote my friend-and he is a friend of mine with a splendid war record-the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross). I shall bring you right up to date, right up to March 13, 1951, when he said that the fact is that the western farmers accepted the wheat board as the agency to sell their wheat. That is correct. At page 1168 of Hansard for March 12, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) stated:
I intend to show that the arrangements in effect during the five years under discussion were in the interests of the western wheat farmer, and that without these arrangements the situation today would be very much less satisfactory than it is. I intend to show that the Canadian and British governments entered into an agreement that was beneficial to both the Canadian producer and the British consumer, and that the terms of that agreement were fully observed on both sides.
In addition I quitp agree with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) when he says that the advantage of hindsight upon which members of the opposition rely so heavily in this debate is far better than any foresight. After all the government did carry Canada through one war, and even though we may disagree with certain ministers of the government at times, they have handled matters since the war in a very capable manner.

You have a right
to express your opinion in the same way that I have the right to express mine, and we always have that right in this House of Commons. In addition the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who I think has the respect of every member of this house regardless of party, said in answer to a question at page 1023 of Hansard for March 8:
The government has taken the position that while there was no further obligation on the United Kingdom in a legal sense, the United Kingdom

Canadian Wheat Board Act authorities should realize that the wheat growers of Canada and most of the community of the prairie provinces believed that there was a continuing obligation under the "have regard to" clause which had not been discharged.
I am not one who flatters anybody but I happen to have a considerable law practice and I think I know something about the law. As I said, I think the Prime Minister has the respect of this house. He has the respect of the lawyers, and he is serving in a capacity where he is earning only one-third of what he could earn outside of this house. I am also satisfied as a westerner born in Saskatchewan of Ontario stock on both sides for five generations that if the wheat crop had been sold under the auspices of the Winnipeg grain exchange-and I am looking at the hon. member for Souris now- it would have been sold over the five-year period at lower prices.
That is my conviction because of trips I made to the city of Winnipeg when I was a boy in knee pants. I visited some of the fine streets, Wellington crescent, and so on-and members from the city of Winnipeg know that city as well as I do and better-and every other place on some of those streets was a hundred thousand dollar home that had been built by some member of the Winnipeg grain exchange. Who paid for it? The farmers of western Canada.
Westerners who have travelled east for many years feel that the cities of Winnipeg, Fort William, Port Arthur, and clean through to Montreal have benefited from the production of western wheat. Sometimes I think that this legislature should conduct a travel trip of easterners from all parts of eastern Canada through the three prairie provinces. I think they would be inclined to agree with me. The Minister of Trade and Commerce would not be in this house and his worthy confrere from the adjoining city would not be here because there would be no Fort William and Port Arthur if it had not been for western Canada. It would not have been possible to elect members from either of those cities.
In so far as the United Kingdom is concerned, if I may be pardoned for saying so, I served with the first division overseas, went through Ypres, the first gas attack, and so on. I am not saying this personally but to show that I certainly cannot be attacked in this house by anyone as being an enemy of Great Britain. The records are all available. I was the first Canadian soldier in the castle of Edinburgh. In the Guildhall they sat me in the Lord Mayor's chair because I was the first Canadian soldier there. You can find that on record. My only brother was killed overseas. I do not think anybody can say that my remarks from now on will be against

Great Britain or anti-British. However, as a westerner I am not satisfied that Great Britain under its socialistic government has played ball, nor am I satisfied with the attitude of the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell) who, if I may be pardoned for saying so, never visited Great Britain during any war and in addition never answered certain questions I was desirous of asking him with respect to the agreement under discussion in this house.
When the final analysis is made the public of Canada will have intense respect for the Prime Minister of this country. They will also have respect for the Minister of Trade and Commerce who demonstrated in one war what can be done in the organization of Canadian industry. In so far as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is concerned, he and I were political opponents at times, and we even got down to a lot of personal terms when we debated. Most of the personal terms came from the Minister of Agriculture, not myself. I think even the hon. member for Souris will agree, however, that if you remove the Minister of Agriculture from public life out west and try to elect somebody else to represent western agriculture you are going to have one fine job replacing him. While I have not at times agreed with him politically, I think everybody in the house knows that he knows his department and that he is quite capable of answering questions connected therewith.
I would label him a professional politician, and we are simply amateurs at the game. I think I speak for western opinion in my constituency. I have carried my constituency both as an independent on several occasions and as a Liberal on the final occasion when I removed the C.C.F. fellow who was there before. I was also interested in the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). I do not think the hon. member has ever been out west, so I am giving him an invitation now to come out and let me show him around.

Just a moment. I do not believe it is the privilege of any hon. member of the Canadian parliament to approach the government of any country on a question of this kind except through the government of his own country.
That statement is ridiculous and incorrect. The hon. member has a perfect right to write to the government of any country, as I have written to the government of Australia, where I was, and as I have written to the government of New Zealand, where I was. Of course it is up to that government whether or not it wants to give you the information. I would also say to the hon. member that it is always the privilege of the hon. member to privately ask the government of another country questions in connection with their administration. I agree that the question of courtesy as between governments comes in, so that there is no misuse of this privilege. However, I am satisfied from the answer of the hon. member that he never made any attempt to persuade his fellow socialists in the government of Great Britain to pay the western producers of wheat one cent more a bushel. If he wants to deny this statement he may rise in his place and do so.
In conclusion may I say that many of our western farmers, particularly those who went through the hungry thirties, may not be completely satisfied with the final payment. However, having regard not only to the "have regard" clause accepted by the British Labour government and later disregarded by that same government, apparently with the implied approval of their counterpart in this country, the C.C.F., labourites will still contend that wheat prices should be kept up and the price of flour kept down. In this case I think the government have exercised good judgment, and I therefore marvel at our Conservative friends, who do not even support the Conservative opposition of Great Britain as against the socialist government over there. If they are really sincere-as I am sure the hon. member for Souris and the hon. member for Cumberland are-instead of riding the government on this wheat agreement they had better get busy and get behind the next British government, and then possibly we will arrive at a proper understanding with Great Britain. We will never get it under a socialist government in that country, which will repudiate as socialists always believe in the repudiation of agreements.

I believe that we in this house, and the people of western Canada, can be very thankful that this government, with only three western members in a cabinet of sixteen, has elected to make a payment of $65 million to the western farmer.
