I do have a little sympathy with the government. I am not so hard-hearted that I cannot begin to look at two sides of the question. It is not easy in these very complicated times to negotiate trade agreements that are going to be one hundred per cent satisfactory all round. We are living in difficult days. We are living in days when we do not know what the value of the dollar and the value of the pound are to be next year or even a few months from now. We notice in today's paper that there is quite a run on the New York stock exchange. It may be just a temporary affair, but who knows what might happen in the next little while? We are living in complicated times.
When the government goes out to negotiate a trade agreement, especially if they desire to look into the future four or five years ahead, and negotiate an agreement on the basis of what might happen in four or five years, they have a difficult task. I do believe that the government might have relied a little bit more on the wheat board to do this trading for them. What has actually happened of course is that the government tied up five years of wheat marketing by a trade agreement signed by them; consequently leaving the wheat board as simply a machine, a rubber stamp, for five years.
The next thing I should like to say is that if the government's case in respect of what might happen two, three, four or five years from the time they signed on the dotted line did not turn out as they expected it would, then they cannot escape the responsibility. That is all there is to it. And if the

western farmer was given to understand that he would get a better deal than he got, then the baby is immediately placed upon the doorstep of this government where it belongs.
I should like to quote one or two views that have been, expressed by some prominent men in Canada. The premiers of some of the provinces cannot be wiped aside when it comes to the expression of their opinions with respect to this final wheat payment. The premiers of the provinces are nobody's fools. They are men who have to deal with big business and some of the provinces are dealing with business almost as large as some of the things with which the Ottawa government has to deal with. Let me quote what Premier Manning said respecting the announcement of the final wheat payment of 8 [DOT] 3 cents, as follows:
The figure announced for final settlement (8-3 cents a bushel additional for the five year period) was a surprise and keen disappointment, and by no stretch of the imagination can be regarded as a fair and equitable settlement.
No matter what the extenuating circumstances, the fact remains that the farmers of western Canada suffered a loss of hundreds of millions of dollars to supply wheat to Britain under the Anglo-Canadian wheat agreement at a figure below prevailing world prices.
The farmers were led to believe that what is known as the "have regard to" clause in the agreement would protect their interests and assure an equitable adjustment to offset any loss sustained.
If the government of the United Kingdom disclaims any obligation to offset this loss, there is an inescapable moral obligation on the government of Canada that negotiated the agreement, to see that our primary producers are not now left to absorb the loss involved.
The meagre adjustment payment now proposed goes but a very short distance toward correcting the wrong.
Next I should like to quote the statement of the premier of Saskatchewan, Mr. Douglas. Although Mr. Douglas is not a farmer, as the horn, member for Springfield [DOT] (Mr. Sinnott) may have desired him to be, I will say that I sat in this house at the same time Mr. Douglas was a member and I could not help but notice that he paid particular attention and gave a great deal of study to the matter of the Canadian wheat board, its operations and the subject of wheat generally. I believe he became more or less an expert for we heard him debate the subject many times when he was here. Mr. Douglas said this:
The farmers will be bitterly disappointed at the amount of the settlement. Two things seem to have been overlooked by the federal government. First, the farmers had $49 million coming to them on the basis of wheat used for domestic consumption which was given the millers at a low price to maintain the price ceiling. This would work out to about 3J cents a bushel. Second, Mr. Gardiner and the federal government agreed in 1946 that if, as a result of the removal of price controls, the cost of production made the price guaranteed

under the agreement inadequate, then some compensatory adjustment would be made in the same manner as was provided under the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
Had these two principles been kept in mind the farmers, in my opinion, would be entitled to anywhere from 15 to 25 cents a bushel on the five-year pool.
That is Mr. Douglas' comment. I should like to read another comment by another man whom some in this house may regard as worthy of speaking on this subject. I refer to Mr. Tucker, the leader of the opposition in the Saskatchewan legislature, who sat in this house as a member. When people make statements in legislatures or in parliament there is sometimes a slight political tinge to them. Human nature being what it is, we have to grant that. Regardless of the fact that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) last night absolved the British government from any responsibility in the matter, a news report quotes Mr. Tucker as follows:
Opposition Leader Walter Tucker said he was glad to hear Ottawa had decided to pay $65 million to the wheat board to bring the final payment to 8'3 cents, but he was disappointed the payment was not going to be considerably higher.
"Unfortunately," said Mr. Tucker, "the British government has finally refused to recognize any further obligation under the 'have regard to' clause. Had the British government paid the same price for wheat supplied under the British contract as other countries paid for Canadian wheat it would have had to pay over $400 million more than it did."
Considering the sacrifices of the British people in the war, Mr. Tucker said he hesitated to speak as strongly about the situation as perhaps he should. But he was satisfied that if the British people knew the exact facts of the case they would repudiate the action of their government in refusing to live up to the spirit of the contract under which they had benefited so greatly.
Mr. Tucker and the Minister of Trade and Commerce had better get together to iron out their differences. There is another thing I want to say in order to keep the record straight. I have not a great deal of use for socialism or for the policies of the British government. But I do not think we can blame the British government for everything. There is one thing that many people do not recognize, that the socialist government of Great Britain inherited a very bad situation. I am not saying whether they made that situation any better or not, but I do say that no matter who had taken over the reins of government in Great Britain at the time Mr. Attlee did they would have had a mighty tough job.
There were forces in the world that were out to wreck Great Britain no matter how they did it. They have done a fair job of wrecking Great Britain economically. the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott) this evening I must confess that I have more reasons than I previously knew of for regretting that I have been unable to attend the sessions for the past few days, because one could only ask: How long has this been going on? It was difficult enough to understand some of the explanations that were given on reading them in the press and hearing condensations over the radio, but they were certainly easy to understand compared with the explanation we received from the hon. member for Springfield as to the reasons which should guide members in dealing with this problem tonight.
The discussion which I have been reading in Hansard, because of my inability to be in the house for the past few days, has related to other matters than those directly in issue on the second reading of the bill before the house which amends the wheat board act. There might be some difference of opinion as to whether a great deal of that discussion has actually been within the ambit of the motion before the house. Nevertheless once the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) took advantage of this debate to make his explanation of the reason for the payment that had been decided upon, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) later decided it was appropriate that he should give another explanation, then obviously this debate took a form which is now established; and we cannot disregard the fact that the main subject under discussion, no matter what may be the contents of the bill now before us, is the contract between the government of Canada and the government of the United Kingdom and the statements that have been made in regard to that contract, its fulfilment or otherwise by the government of the United Kingdom and the arrangements that have been made by this government to meet whatever losses have resulted to the farmers of western Canada.
If there is one thing that has emerged very clearly from the discussions in the house today-and they are the first discussions I have actually heard in this debate-it is that there is the utmost confusion as to what is really in issue. The discussion has related to the contract, whether it has been carried out by the government of Great Britain, and whether the arrangements being made are adequate having regard to the terms of the contract. It seems to me essential that we keep clearly in mind that the payment announced in this house last week by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is not a payment under the contract at all. The
[Mr. Hansell.)

announcement made it perfectly clear that the payment of $65 million is to wind up the five year wheat pool. How that figure was arrived at he did not explain. Reference was made to the fact that a balance of $65 million remained of the loan to Great Britain, which the government of Great Britain had not taken up. However, there was no attempt to explain the process by which that figure was arrived at. Surely before the members of this house should be asked to express an opinion as to whether that or any other sum is an appropriate figure the government should place before this house the basis upon which they made their computations and the calculations which resulted in the figure they have adopted. It is meaningless to suggest that it is adequate or inadequate so far as the government is concerned unless we know how they worked it out, unless we know how they arrived at this arithmetical calculation.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture are as far apart as two ministers of the same government ever could have been in explaining the same transaction. The Minister of Agriculture has given one explanation regarding what has happened; the Minister of Trade and Commerce has given another. In the explanation of the Minister of Agriculture the implication was clear that the government of Great Britain had failed to live up to its agreement. In fact the implication went further than that and even suggested that consideration had been given to carrying this question to the international court of justice. There would have been no reason for a reference to the possibility of taking this before the international court of justice unless that had been considered by this government. That is an extremely serious imputation.	It is an
extremely serious charge. It leaves an impression in the minds of the members of this house and in the minds ef the people of Canada that our oldest partner, the nation upon which we have looked as the model of integrity under our form of parliamentary government, cannot in fact be relied upon to carry out its word. For that reason I think the members of this house and the people of Canada generally will welcome the statement last night by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that in his opinion the British government had in no way defaulted under the terms of this contract. But the members of this house and the people of Canada are left in the unsatisfactory position that they do not know which minister is making the statement on behalf of the government that we are supposed to accept.

I hope it will not be suggested that any uncertainty has been removed, because in this house this evening we have heard the suggestion repeated that there has been default. The hon. member who repeated that did so with appropriate safeguards to his own reputation for belief in the integrity of the government of the United Kingdom; but he made it perfectly clear that in his opinion there had been some substantial measure of default. Reference was made by the last speaker to a statement made only a few days ago in Saskatchewan by the leader of one of the parties in that province, which indicated quite clearly that he had gained the same impression and that in his opinion there was default under the terms of this contract.
If there was no default, if there was no obligation, moral or otherwise, on the part of the government of Great Britain to make any further payment than has been made, then naturally it is necessary for hon. members to know the principle under which that payment is being made, and also the principle under which substantially larger amounts are being claimed. At this point let me say I am convinced that every hon. member of this house is anxious to do what can be done to see that the farmers of western Canada and in fact all agricultural producers in Canada are dealt with fairly whenever the government assumes a direct measure of responsibility for the amount of money they shall receive. The obligation of this government would not end even if no further payment were due under this contract. Unquestionably there is a moral obligation on the part of the government. It must be remembered that the wheat taken over for the purpose of fulfilling this contract was taken over under compulsion. I find it difficult to believe that, at a time when this government is assuming such sweeping powers to take over any material that may be required under the present emergency, in fact to demand any services which may be regarded as necessary to meet the requirements of this emergency, members would not wish to be sure that those services and those materials are going to be paid for fairly and justly by this government. For that reason we should recognize the moral obligation that must always exist where the government compels the delivery of any commodity or any service to pay what properly should be paid for that commodity, that material or that service.
Therefore, no matter what the terms of the contract with Britain may have been, a contract between the government of Canada and the government of Great Britain and not a contract between this government and the
1226	HOUSE OF
Canadian Wheat Board Act farmers of Canada, it is the duty of the government of Canada to recognize its moral obligation to compensate the farmers fairly for what has been delivered to the government., The farmers did not negotiate this contract. That fact seems to be overlooked in a great deal of the discussion. The farmers had nothing whatever to do with the terms of this contract. Whether or not they approved or otherwise at a later date, individually or through any of their organizations, is apart from the point. The contract was negotiated between the government of Canada and the government of Great Britain. The Canadian government took the responsibility of compelling delivery of the wheat which would be necessary to carry out the terms of that contract.
What is the figure that would properly compensate the farmers of western Canada? What is the moral obligation? Mr. Speaker, I submit that nothing has been placed before the hon. members of this house to show what that figure is. Is it fifty cents a bushel? Is it twenty-five cents a bushel? Is it ten cents a bushel? Is it five cents a bushel? Certainly there has been nothing put before this house to show how the figure of 8-3 cents per bushel was arrived at. This is not something to be dealt with in a casual manner. At a time when the people of this country are being asked to pay large sums in taxes, the government, which has already taken such sweeping powers over personal services- as well as materials and products of this country, should give us a great deal more information about this than we have today.
Last night the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), in a speech which was carefully prepared to place before this house and the people of Canada his position in regard to that contract for which he has quite willingly assumed at all times the major responsibility so far as can be discerned in this house, presented argument after argument to show why in his opinion this was a good contract. At no point in the speech he made, which I have read quite carefully today, did he even suggest any reason for a payment beyond the payment provided for by the contract itself. Does the Minister of Trade and Commerce believe that the western farmers have received all that they should receive? So far as his speech last night is concerned, we have no evidence that he believes that anything further should be paid. But his speech went -a great deal further than that. Over and over again last night he not only explained why he thought this contract, under all the circumstances, was a contract that was eminently fair to the farmers of western Canada, but he also


emphasized the fact that the British government had fully lived up to the terms of that contract; that they were in default in no way.
If that is so, then there seems to be only one member of the government from whom we can receive the information which we should have, and that is the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). We have the extraordinary situation of the two senior members of this government, other than the Prime Minister, giving to this house and the people of Canada an entirely different interpretation of the reason for the course that is being followed by the government at this time. In fact I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce in his closing words left an impression which could well have been left in the first place on behalf of the government, if in fact that is the position that the government takes. These were his words, and I quote from page 1173 of Hansard for March 12:
... I am very happy the agreement was made. 1 am happy the way it has worked out, and I deplore the suggestion that the British government has not played fair with the Canadian people.
If that is his position, and he has made it clear on a number of occasions that it is the position he wishes this house to accept, then surely the Minister of Trade and Commerce would not be the one to explain to us just how this figure was arrived at, and just what the governing factors were which led to the arithmetical calculation.
